title: Point Estimation On The Circle
notes: Open by saying that point estimation on a circle starts with a contract, not with a formula. The zero angle is arbitrary, so any estimator worth using must rotate with the data. This chapter asks how that contract shapes von Mises location, concentration, wrapped Cauchy weighting, and mixture fitting.

title: The Estimator Must Respect Rotation
notes: Use the commutative diagram as the guiding rule for the whole lecture. Rotating the sample before fitting should give the same result as fitting first and then rotating the fitted direction. Concentration is different: it measures clustering strength, so it should remain unchanged under a common rotation.

title: The Resultant Is The Data Geometry
notes: Explain that the sample is first moved to unit vectors, then summarized by the average complex vector. Its direction is the natural circular mean, and its length is the concentration signal. The diagram intentionally avoids an angle line, because the circle, not the cut coordinate, carries the statistic.

title: Von Mises Likelihood Splits The Job
notes: Walk through the log likelihood as two linked problems. For a fixed concentration, maximizing over direction means aligning with the resultant vector. After that alignment, the concentration score asks for the model mean resultant length A(kappa) to match the observed Rbar.

title: Concentration Comes From Inverting A
notes: Make the Bessel-ratio curve the main object. Students often expect concentration to be a sample variance formula, but the von Mises model uses the monotone relationship between kappa and expected resultant length. Numerical inversion is not a nuisance here; it is the statistical definition made executable.

title: The Likelihood Surface Confirms The Split
notes: Use the notebook artifact as evidence that the estimating equations are not just symbolic. The peak sits where the resultant direction and the A-inverse concentration agree. The surface is drawn in mu and kappa coordinates so a later rotation test can literally slide the peak sideways.

title: Small Samples Inflate Concentration
notes: Emphasize that Rbar itself is a length and the inverse A transform is nonlinear. This is why raw kappa estimates can be optimistic for small samples. The notebook simulation gives a concrete scale: at n equals 8 and true kappa equals 2, the raw bias is large while the correction nearly removes it.

title: Circular Unbiasedness Is Not Linear Unbiasedness
notes: Pause on the sine-error diagnostic because it prevents a common mistake. A signed angle error depends on where the branch cut is placed, so it is not a stable criterion. Taking the sine of the wrapped error asks whether the estimator is centered on the circle without pretending angles form a line.

title: Wrapped Cauchy Estimation Reweights Vectors
notes: Frame wrapped Cauchy fitting as another version of the same geometry. The current parameter sits inside the unit disk, and the observations receive weights determined by their circular relationship to it. The update is a weighted vector average, so the computation stays on circular objects.

title: Mixtures Replace Hard Assignment With Responsibilities
notes: Describe the EM loop without reducing it to generic clustering. Each component has a circular density, and each observation receives responsibilities that sum to one. The M step then performs weighted circular estimation for each component, which keeps the fit invariant to the angular cut.

title: Responsibility Geometry Is Visible
notes: Use the second notebook artifact to connect the wrapped Cauchy and mixture stories. On the left, weights pull a disk parameter along a path; on the right, responsibilities color observations by component membership. Both panels show that estimation is mediated by circular weights, not by raw linear residuals.

title: Rotation Lab: The Origin Should Disappear
notes: Show this as the practical acceptance test for the implementation. The sample is rotated by several deltas, then refit. The fitted direction changes by exactly the same delta, while concentration and corresponding likelihood values stay fixed up to numerical precision.

title: Estimator Pipeline
notes: Turn the chapter into a reproducible workflow. Wrap angles before comparing, compute the resultant, solve the concentration equation, apply small-sample corrections when needed, and use weighted circular updates for wrapped Cauchy or mixtures. Each step has a geometry check attached to it.

title: Diagnostics That Guard The Fit
notes: The checks are part of the lecture evidence. They verify that the score is small at the fit, that A(kappa hat) matches Rbar, that mixture responsibilities normalize, that wrapped Cauchy weights remain valid, and that generated artifacts are nonblank. These are mathematical tests, not only software tests.

title: Mistakes To Catch Early
notes: Use this warning slide to make students skeptical of familiar linear shortcuts. Averaging degree values across a branch cut, plugging a line variance into concentration, forgetting to wrap residuals, or treating mixture labels as fixed can all give plausible-looking but geometrically wrong estimates.

title: What The Chapter Adds
notes: Close by tying the lecture back to the course arc. Earlier chapters built circular summaries and model families; this chapter turns them into estimators. The unifying principle is that parameters should be fitted through unit-vector geometry and checked by equivariance, score equations, and responsibility normalization.
